About: LC Oscillations

Source

Topic
Electromagnetic Induction — free oscillation of an ideal LC circuit
Simulation
A capacitor charged to V0 discharges through a pure inductor. The circuit is IDEAL: R = 0 exactly, so the oscillation never decays. A real coil has resistance and the swings die away — that case is the damped LCR circuit, not simulated here.
Concept
q(t) = q0cos ω0t and I(t) = −q0ω0sin ω0t with ω0 = 1/√(LC): current is largest exactly where charge vanishes. Energy shuttles between q²/2C and ½LI² while the sum stays fixed.
Inquiry
Predict what the charge does after the switch closes — drain away and stop, or come back the other way?
Misconception
“The capacitor discharges and that is the end of it.” That is what a resistor would give. The inductor's magnetic field carries the current past q = 0 and recharges the plates with the opposite sign.

Guided Inquiry

1 · The circuit

A capacitor charged to V0 is wired straight across a coil of inductance L. There is no resistor anywhere in the loop.

q is the charge on the capacitor, I the current through the coil. The switch closes when the clock starts — press ▶ Play.

2 · Predict — after the switch closes

The capacitor starts fully charged. What does its charge q do from then on?

3 · Predict — the instant the plates are empty

Take an instant when the capacitor's charge is exactly zero. What is the current in the coil then?

4 · Predict — the two energies together

UE in the capacitor and UB in the coil both rise and fall. What does their sum do?

5 · Predict — a bigger capacitor

The capacitance C is doubled and L is left alone. What happens to the period T?

6 · One sentence

An LC circuit is a mass on a spring built out of fields: L is the inertia, 1/C the stiffness, charge the displacement and current the velocity.

This one is ideal. A real coil has resistance, so a real circuit's swings shrink and die away.

The Physics

LC Oscillations — Charge, Current and the Energy See-Saw · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A capacitor charged to a voltage V₀ is wired straight across a coil, with no resistor anywhere in the loop. The sim plots the charge, current and energies against time.

What you'll learn

  • How the charge and the current behave once the loop is closed.
  • How the energies in the capacitor and the coil are related.
  • How the period depends on the inductance L and the capacitance C.
  • Why this circuit has the same equation as a mass on a spring.
The capacitor starts with voltage V₀. The loop contains only the capacitor and the coil.

What's on screen

  • Capacitor and charge q (cyan): the plates with + and − signs, and the q graph.
  • Current I (dashed amber): the arrows on the side wires, and the I graph.
  • Coil and energies (pink): the coil, and the bars and graph for the energy UE in the capacitor and UB in the coil.
  • Spring and mass (violet): a mechanical twin drawn under the circuit.
See itStart the circuit with the opening values, L = 0.10 H, C = 20 µF, V₀ = 12 V. Watch for: the plates drawn with + and − signs, and the cyan q curve starting at 240 µC.

03

The charge goes through zero and reverses

At the start the capacitor holds q₀ = CV₀ and no current flows. When the loop closes, the plates begin to discharge through the coil. The coil resists any change in its current, so the current builds up smoothly instead of jumping.

When the plates are empty, the coil's current is still flowing. It keeps pushing charge round the loop and charges the plates the other way, with + and − swapped. The charge then drains again and returns to q₀.

q(t) = q₀ cos ω₀t
With no resistor to remove energy, this repeats for ever.

At the opening values, q₀ = 20 µF × 12 V = 240 µC, and the charge returns to 240 µC after 8.89 ms.

See itLet the opening run play for one cycle. Watch for: the signs on the plates swapping sides as the q curve crosses zero and goes down to −240 µC.
04

The current peaks where the charge is zero

The current is the rate at which charge flows, so on the q graph it is the slope. The slope is steepest where q crosses zero and flat at the peaks, so the two curves are a quarter of a cycle apart.

I(t) = −q₀ω₀ sin ω₀t
The sign of I only says which way it flows round the loop.
  • When q is at its largest, I = 0: the current is turning round.
  • When q = 0, the size of I is at its largest, q₀ω₀. At the opening values that is 240 µC × 707 s⁻¹ ≈ 170 mA.
See itRun the opening values for a quarter cycle. Watch for: the amber I curve reaching its extreme where the cyan q curve crosses zero, and the T/4 bracket between the two.
05

The energy moves but the total stays fixed

The capacitor stores energy UE = q²/(2C) in its electric field. The coil stores UB = ½LI² in its magnetic field. Because ω₀² = 1/(LC), these two add up to the same value at every instant:

UE + UB = q₀² / (2C)
UE = q₀²cos²ω₀t / 2C and UB = q₀²sin²ω₀t / 2C.

Nothing is dissipated, so energy only moves between the two fields. Each store fills and empties twice per cycle. At the opening values the total is ½ × 20 µF × (12 V)² = 1.44 mJ. It grows as V₀²: at 16 V it is 2.56 mJ.

See itWatch the bars on the left for one cycle. Watch for: the pink UB bar growing as the cyan UE bar shrinks, with their sum bar staying at 1.44 mJ.
06

The period depends on L and C, like a mass on a spring

The loop obeys L d²q/dt² + q/C = 0, the same equation as m d²x/dt² + kx = 0 for a mass on a spring. The matching gives the natural frequency and the period:

ω₀ = 1/√(LC)    T = 2π√(LC)
The starting voltage V₀ does not appear.
CircuitSpring
inductance L↔mass m
1/C↔stiffness k
charge q↔position x
current I↔velocity v

A larger L is more "inertia", and a larger C is a softer spring, so both make the swing slower. Doubling either one multiplies T by √2.

See itSet C = 10 µF, half the opening value, and compare with 8.89 ms. Watch for: T in the read-outs dropping to 6.28 ms, a factor of √2 less.
07

Where it matters

  • Radio tuning. A tuner is an LC circuit whose frequency 1/(2π√(LC)) is matched to one station by changing C. A 200 µH coil with a 100 pF capacitor rings at about 1.1 MHz, inside the AM band.
  • Oscillators and transmitters. An LC circuit is the simplest source of a steady alternating signal. A real one loses energy to resistance and needs a power source to keep it going.
  • Real circuits. A real coil has resistance, so the swings shrink. That is the damped LCR circuit, which this sim does not show.
08

Summary

In one line. In an ideal LC circuit the starting charge q₀ = CV₀, the inductance L and the capacitance C decide the charge, the current, the energies and the period.

Key points

  • q and I are a quarter cycle apart.
  • UE and UB trade energy, and their sum q₀²/2C does not change.
  • T = 2π√(LC), and V₀ has no effect on it.

Common mix-ups

  • "The capacitor empties and that is the end of it." That is what a resistor gives. The coil's current carries on past q = 0.
  • "The current is largest when the charge is largest." It is the other way round: I is zero at the charge peaks and largest in size when q = 0.
  • "A bigger V₀ makes the circuit swing faster." V₀ sets the size of q, I and the energy. T depends only on L and C.

Things to try on your own

  • Find two different pairs of L and C that give the same period.
  • Change V₀ from 8 V to 16 V and compare the read-out energies: by what factor do they differ?
  • Set L = 0.20 H and C = 30 µF, the slowest setting, and count how many cycles fit in the 36 ms axis.
